title:
BioMetaEvo-GNN: A Meta-Governance and Meta-Evolutionary Framework for Community Intelligence and Multi-Objective Community Detection via Bayesian Fourier Learning and T-Cell
Defense Dynamics
content: Community detection in real-world graphs frequently encounters obstacles such as noisy edges, ambiguous node attributes, assignment drift due to perturbations, unstable community boundaries, and dynamic graph architectures. Current neural community identification and robust graph learning techniques often emphasize either clean-graph clustering accuracy or node-level resilience, although they seldom offer a cohesive framework for modeling spectral uncertainty, implementing immune-inspired defenses, preserving memory, and facilitating adaptive governance. To address these limitations, this paper proposes BioMetaEvo-GNN, a bio-inspired meta-evolutionary graph neural framework for robust and uncertainty-aware community detection. The proposed framework amalgamates GNN-based representation learning, Bayesian Fourier learning, energy-time filtering, Bio-Phase Selection, T-cell defense dynamics, T-SILE immune memory, UCB-based meta-governance, stage-transition control, incremental growth, and multi-objective replacement into a closed-loop community intelligence process. Bayesian Fourier learning detects spectrum instability and drift-prone community boundaries, while immune-inspired defense suppresses unreliable community transitions and maintains stable historical evidence. The UCB governance module selectively determines actions for defense, augmentation, transfer, replacement, growth, or stabilization based on signals of uncertainty, reward, and stability. Comprehensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic graphs indicate that BioMetaEvo-GNN enhances community detection accuracy, perturbation resilience, uncertainty calibration, assignment stability, cross-dataset transferability, and diagnostic interpretability in comparison to representative GNN, robust GNN, and stochastic propagation baselines. The findings indicate that community identification need to be seen not merely as a static graph clustering endeavor, but also as a resilient, uncertainty-conscious, and governance-adaptive reliability challenge.
